source: I wish I could. Just die—sleep, sleep, and maybe dream... that would be it. Who knows what I might dream of in death?
What do you think... Ophelia?
All this fortune coming your way, and still you wax philosophical?
It's not in my nature to be pleased with things like this. You know that.
Of course. But I might suggest that, as the future ruler of Denmark, you have greater worries than your own mortality to contend with.
Let death claim you when it's time. There's nothing to fear in it.
(Certainly I know that.)
You've become wise. Wiser than you were before.
Do you—do you think you could lend me your aid, Ophelia?
I'm afraid of what happens next. I don't know how to rule.
If there were someone who could show me how, give me advice...
I'd trust only you to find that person and send them to me.
I'll see what I can do.
Hamlet, I can't listen to you go on like this. Not anymore. There are still things of yours in my room. I'd prefer you took them back.
Honest as always, and ever so naïve! I loved you once for those very qualities.
I believed it.
You shouldn't have.
Then I was the more deceived.
You'd be better off as a nun. You'd make an excellent nun, you know.
Don't involve yourself with men like me. We're all alike, deep down.
And some day, some man will crumple you like a flower underfoot.
Maybe we should do away with marriage altogether. No good has ever come from it, or ever will.
You were a fool if you truly believed me. Ophelia, I never loved you.
(I don't believe that. I don't even think he believes that. But he's in a fit.)
Mmm, I'll forego opinion on this one.
(I'd rather actually become a nun than suffer this again.)
Thank you for coming, Lords and Ladies.
I, your humble Playmaster, have arranged a most magnificent show for you tonight!
And with my many-changing faces... I aim to please all who look upon me.
So, without further ado... a tale of tragedy and woe:
The Murder of Gonzago!
I don't think we've seen this one before, have we, my love?
...It's not familiar to me, no.
I, for one, am thoroughly excited.
(Horatio, keep a close eye on Claudius. Watch his face for me.)
(Certainly. But why...?)
...Our tale, my friends, takes us to the fair city of Vienna, where King Gonzago and his wife, Baptista, are not-so-happily wed...!
My King, let us count a thousand journeys of the sun and moon again before our love be done!
Oh, my love. I must leave you soon. My form is weak, and frail. And thou shalt live in this fair world behind.
But never fear: A new husband you shall find!
Oh, confound the rest! Loving anyone else would be treason in my breast.
The only women who can love a second husband must surely have killed the first!
...Naturally, Gonzago's evil brother, Lucianus, has something more sinister in mind. He plans to steal his brother's crown for himself.
Wah hah hah! None of you shall sit upon the throne but I, Lucianus!
Lucianus poisons his own brother as he lies sleeping in the garden.
Die, you old fool! Once and for all.
What do you call this play, again, Gerta?
I-- I cannot recall.
The Queen comes across the body of her dead husband...
My love, my King, please awaken from your slumber and hold me—
My love? Why are your lips so pale? And your cheeks so white?
Oh... oh, he's dead!
(What is this performance? Who organized this?)
(Hamlet, stop the performance. Haven't you seen what you meant to—)
(Shh. Here's the important part.)
Now as King, the evil Lucianus swoops in to retrieve his prize: the Queen!
Come now, Queen Baptista, to the altar we must hurry...
I protest! I'll never love you!
But... milady!
How can I ever love another after Gonzago?
What do you think, Mother?
The lady protests too much.
I need to leave.
I feel ill. I need to leave now.
Cancel the play.
The entire play?
...Well, that was odd.
Hush, Horatio.
Everyone, we'll have sweetmeats served in the grand hall shortly. Nothing to worry about!
I knew it.
Did you see his face, Horatio? I'll take that spirit's word for a thousand pounds.
I saw it too.
He's gone and run off. I'm going to pursue him.
I have to know the truth, one way or another.
(Now where did he run off to? I have to know the truth, one way or another.)
For some reason, Claudius was deeply upset by that play.
So, without further ado... A saucy tale, of betrayal and scandal:
The Greedy Mistress!
The title alone gives me pause. Is this appropriate, my dear...?
Nonsense! This sounds like a riotous amusement! Carry forth!
What? 'The Greedy Mistress?' That's not what I intended to...
Well, let's see where this goes.
Our play begins in the court of an ancient kingdom, where a fair King lies sleeping as his Queen flits away on slippered feet...
...Down to the stable, where she meets with another man. Not only that—the King's own brother, right under his nose!
We must tell no one. Not a single whisper, my love.
You won't have time to whisper with your mouth under mine!
They make the 'beast with two backs' in every conceivable location, ladies and lords, in sunshine and shade, in filth and in wealth!
What if my husband should find us?
Then he'll know that my love for you burns brighter than anything in this world—and that I am unafraid.
I have stolen his most prized possession. Why should I worry? I have won!
T-this is—this is awful!
When the Queen's own son leaves for faraway lands, she even makes love to her brother-in-law on her son's bed, knowing the door is locked tight!
Both men have been in my body... their flesh is my flesh, their lust is my love...!
Oh, my illicit queen—I'd ravish you anywhere. Yes—even here!
This is quite inappropriate! Excuse me—stop this!
Y-yes, it's, er...
I'm feeling faint. Please. Haven't any of you a single shred of mercy?
Or have you each been laughing at me all this time?
Hamlet. Aren't you going to defend her?
While I may not have penned the sordid story myself... I can't say I disagree.
She's been everywhere and back in the months I was gone, Horatio. Who knows what she's done?
What the hell did you say? Louder, boy!
Ergh. Even for Hamlet, this is too much.
What good could come from hurting the Queen?
I've no reason to back down now.
You heard precisely what I said, Claudius.
My mother is a whore. And now, thanks to this play, the whole castle knows it. Not that they didn't already.
How dare you.
You would tell lies like this in front of my court? In front of my wife?
Draw your sword.
Only if you promise it'll be a fair fight, usurper.
No! Please—!
The law of the kingdom is that treason is punishable by death, or by cutting of the tongue.
Naturally, I prefer to do things the old-fashioned way.
That's if you win.
Yes. If.
I'll be glad to avenge Father's dignity against you then. Certainly no one else in this world has.
All right, Hamlet. En garde.
Bernardo, you'll oversee the duel.
(My lord, are you sure this is wise? Your nephew?)
I did not ask for your advice.
Hamlet. You still have time to stand down. Recant what you said.
This is between him and me. Leave us.
He is my friend, milord. Please.
He murdered my favorite advisor. He embarrassed my wife.
He's embarrassed my wife, and he's embarrassed me.
Interfere, Bernardo, and I'll have you duel him to the death in my place.
How could it all... is this... really happening?
If it wasn't for this sad excuse for a prince, my love would still be alive.
He deserves everything that is coming to him.
Let's begin. I'm not afraid anymore.
On three.
One. Two.
My wife is avenged. He went down like a half-wit. Not even a single parry.
Oh, my God, no—
I can't look. I can't—I—
I... please, Claudius, please let me have the body to bury.
So Her Majesty needn't see her son like this.
I beg of you.
Fine. Take it. Useless bit of decomposing flesh to me now.
Bernardo, help me with him. Please.
Gather his sword.
It is done.
My baby.
My only son.
My love. Come here. Let me dry your tears.
Don't you dare call to me. Don't even touch me.
How dare you!
You killed him. You murdered our son. No—not our son. My son.
Good riddance to that scourge.
My lady...
Well? Isn't someone going to follow her?
The death falls hard upon her, my lord. Perhaps—
Stop! The rest of you handle his body. I'll follow her.
I never thought this night could end like this.
And with my many-changing faces, I aim to please all who look upon me!
So, without further ado, a comedy of errors:
The Stone Prince!
No, but it sounds quite entertaining!
What... what is this?
This isn't what I wanted!
My lord, are you all right?
No. I'm not. But it's too late now.
We come across a young prince lost in a dark place.
His father, you see, was murdered by a vengeful rival, cut down in the prime of his life!
And yet here the prince sits, overcome with his own thoughts, unable to even lift his sword to action.
He rests his chin upon his fist, back hunched as though from years of labor. Yet for all his father's years of toil, he has none!
Is this... about me?
Centuries pass, and the young man turns to stone. Meanwhile, his father's usurper storms the castle, stealing the throne.
The prince's men go to him and shake him, begging him to rise and fight. But it is then they realize: He is no longer a man of flesh, but of stone!
And the stone prince is carried to the basement to gather dust.
Ha! Excellent, excellent! What a clown!
This isn't funny.
None of this is funny in the slightest.
Oh, come, Hamlet. Don't be so sensitive.
The only cause I would have to take offense from it were if you thought it was fact, not fiction.
Well, the portrayal of the young man certainly resonates, at the very least!
Why, if these four walls were falling down around you, you'd still sit there paralyzed with fright!
Don't be so easily offended. You really are such a child.
...And you really are a monster.
Indeed, after all these years I've never seen you for who you are so vividly before.
Dearest, please. Both of you. I think that's enough.
Well, that was odd.
And with my many-changing faces, I aim to please all who look upon me.
